Shorter words carry only the main stress. Non-iterating; no weight condition.

Within this domain, downdrift (or automatic downstep) applies: high tones after a low or falling tone are automatically realized on a lower pitch than any…

2965.prule: No word stress or accent position is described. Sandawe is analysed as a lexical two-level tone language (underlying H and L on the mora [HHE 2008, Elderkin 1989] or syllable [Steeman 2012], plus rising/falling contours as sequences of level tones), with downstep, downdrift and rightward tone spread inside the phonological word and word-level pitch registers ('tone levels') set by syntax and information structure. The only mention of stress in any source is that the stressed penultimate syllable of Swahili loans is rendered as a Sandawe high tone flanked by lows.
2965.quote: [HHE 2008 p. 51] The assignment of tone to Swahili borrowings in Sandawe shows a tendency for translating the stressed penultimate syllable in Swahili into a high toned syllable in Sandawe. The preceding and following tones are assigned low tone. Thus a word such as kijiji ‘village’, in which the second syllable is stressed, becomes /kìdʒídʒî/ L-H-L. [Eaton 2010 p. 10] Sandawe has two underlying tone levels: high /´/ and low /`/. A low tone preceded by a high tone causes the tone of any following high tone to be downstepped and occur as a mid tone on the surface level. [Steeman 2012 p. 37] To…

2965.tone: All five first-hand descriptions treat Sandawe as a tone language and none posits stress or accent. HHE 2008 ch. 4 (pp. 28-60): underlying H and L, mora as tone-bearing unit, tone melodies on monomorphemic words, rightward tone spread restricted to non-word-final morae, downstep of H after L to mid. Eaton 2010 p. 10: two underlying tone levels, downstep, surface low-level vs low-falling distinction word-finally; rising tones only on long vowels, contours analysed as sequences of level tones. Steeman 2012 sec. 2.4 (pp. 37-52): two level tones plus a rising contour, syllable as TBU, tone constant in roots, downdrift/downstep within the phonological word. Elderkin 1989: mora as unit of length and TBU, each mora H or L, downstep and downdrift, word pitch 'tone levels' assigned by syntax and information structure. Kagaya 1993 intro sec. 2: 'this language is one of the tone languages, and there are four tones' (H, L, rising, falling, plus a possible fifth mid/downstepped H); Kagaya also notes the vowel of a word-initial syllable tends to be pronounced long in isolation. The word 'stress' appears in HHE 2008 only in the Swahili-loan sentence (p. 51); in Eaton 2010 and Steeman 2012 'prominence' is discourse/morphological marking (Eaton sec. 12.4; Steeman ATT marker) and 'stress' is the ordinary verb; Elderkin 1989 has no prosodic use of 'stress'/'accent' in 9,984 scan lines.

2966.dq: el acento siempre se encuentra en la primera sílaba de la raíz independientemente del carácter polimorfémico de la palabra. Lo anterior se mantiene tanto en el caso de raíces sustantivas en (20) como verbales en (21).
2966.heavy: not applicable: the rule makes no reference to syllable weight (vowel length is contrastive in roots, §2.1.2, but the stress statement does not mention it).
2966.prule: Stress ('acento') is non-contrastive, lexically or grammatically, and is obligatorily assigned to the first syllable of the lexical ROOT, whatever prefixes or inflectional formatives precede it: ˈsíni 'dog', ˈnú 'head', nèˈsíni 'the dogs', thèˈsínwèwi 'my two dogs', téˈšùti 'to bathe', kùˈtǝwi 'he sings'. Position is anchored to the root (morpheme class), not to the word edge; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed. Not computable from the word's syllable count.
2966.srule: Not mentioned in Carranza 2013, §2.1.3 'El acento' (pp. 14-15) and §2.1.4 'El tono' (pp. 15-17): every phonetic form carries a single stress mark on the root-initial syllable (e.g. 4-syllable [thèˈsínwèwi]); no secondary or rhythmic stress is discussed.

2966.exq_: se asigna obligatoriamente a la primera sílaba de la raíz de la palabra ... el acento siempre se encuentra en la primera sílaba de la raíz independientemente del carácter polimorfémico de la palabra.
2966.tone: Tonal language with stress described as a separate, predictable property. §2.1.4 (p. 16): 'la lengua matlatzinca es una lengua tonal − el tono tiene función léxica y gramatical−, cuyo sistema consta de 2 tonos fonológicos: un tono alto... y un tono bajo' (abbreviated A = alto and B = bajo by the author); 'todas las raíces reciben tono en la primer sílaba; en raíces bisilábicas la segunda sílaba solo exhibe tonía, la lengua no presenta raíces trisilábicas'; in polysyllabic words roots keep their tone and affixes may carry tone except word-final suffixes (fn. 4 notes some tone sandhi needing further study). Older conflicting analysis: Cazes 1971 (JSA 60: 199-200) treats 'acento' as primary and derives syllable tone from position relative to the accent ('El tono de la silaba dépende de la relación de esta con el acento'), with affixes bearing a fixed accent or none, root accent shifting to avoid clash (nsíni 'perro', nísiní 'tu perro'), and disyllables accented on 1st or 2nd syllable (mbaani, kaki vs imó). Cazes's 'acento' corresponds to what the modern literature (Carranza 2013, 2015; Palancar & Carranza 2021, 2022) analyses as H tone, so it is recorded as a historical alternative, not as a competing current stress rule.

tn.quote: Hay tres tonos en el popoloca, Por ejemplo la palabra jna puede tener tres significados con sólo el cambio de tono: jná "vamos", jna "picante" jnā "ayer". El tono alto está escrito con el guión inclinado hacia arriba ´ . El tono medio se dejó sin símbolo, y el tono bajo está escrito con el guión horizontal ¯ . Los tonos se escribe siempre sobre las vocales, pues abarca la sílaba entera. Cuando ocurren dos vocales juntas de dos distintos tonos, los tonos se deslizan rapidamente de la una a la otra vocal, como en las siguientes palabras: xíī "hombre", kjōóⁿ "mañana".
tn.translation: There are three tones in Popoloca. For example the word jna can have three meanings with only the change of tone: jná 'let's go', jna 'hot (spicy)', jnā 'yesterday'. The high tone is written with the stroke slanting upward ´. The mid tone was left without a symbol, and the low tone is written with the horizontal stroke ¯. The tones are always written over the vowels, since it [the tone] covers the whole syllable. When two vowels of two different tones occur together, the tones glide rapidly from the one to the other vowel, as in the following words: xíī 'man', kjōóⁿ 'tomorrow'.

2969.dloc: Livre I, ch.5 'Considérations générales sur l'accent en sangu' and ch.6 'Place de l'accent en sangu': thesis p.117-118 §2.61-2.62, p.120 §2.63, p.123 §3 heading, p.133-134 §2.80-2.82, p.135-136 §2.83-2.84, p.139 §2.86-2.87. rendered from the PDF.
2969.heavy: The accentable unit is the mora, not the syllable; a long vowel is represented as two geminate vowels, each a mora (§2.64, p.121: 'Chaque geminée devient alors une unité accentuable, c'est-à-dire une more'). No closed syllables in the language as described; prenasalised onsets do not add morae in the examples (ingwaada, inkwaale).
2969.dflt: antepenultimate syllable (all-short-vowel words: umugogolo, ilifugamilo, kijova, wajovile, uxajovile); two-mora forms take the penultimate mora (sina, limo, baho)
2969.prule: One pitch accent ('accent de hauteur': higher pitch, not intensity) per accentual unit, where every nominal, pronominal or verbal form (word) is an accentual unit and a functional (connective, determinative) joins the following form; the accent-bearing unit is the mora, a long vowel counting two. Default position = the antepenultimate mora (540 of 600 non-verbal words; all verb forms and infinitives), which in syllable terms is the penultimate syllable when its vowel is long (umwaana, umuguunda, kitaana) and the antepenultimate syllable otherwise (umugogolo, kijova, wajovile). Non-verbal placement is lexical (minority classes on the penultimate mora or on the mora immediately before the radical); verbal placement is grammatical (antepenultimate mora unless advanced one or two morae by listed morphological conditions).
2969.srule: None: 'il n'y a en sangu qu'un seul segment à la fois de l'unité accentuelle qui puisse être touché par un trait prosodique pertinent' / 'il y a toujours un accent, et un seul, par unité accentuelle' (one pitch accent per word; no secondary or rhythmic accent described in ch.5-6).

2969.tone: Bilodeau 1979 explicitly classifies Sangu as an accent language, not a tone language (§3, p.123), and the accent as a pitch accent (hauteur, not intensité; likened to Serbo-Croatian against German/Russian intensity accent, §2.63), culminative (one per accentual unit), mora-borne, realised as higher pitch on a short vowel, falling contour on the first mora and rising contour on the second mora of a long vowel (§2.65-2.66, p.121). Kaajan 2012 (VU Amsterdam MA thesis; only the academia.edu landing-page captions were readable) re-analyses the same facts as a 'restricted tone language' with a regular antepenultimate high tone shifting to the penultimate mora with cl.1/9 subjects in a-/-ile paradigms, citing Schadeberg 1973 on Kinga. Heese 1919-20 (ZES 10: 88, 'Die Akzente') reports a 'Hauptakzent' with no good rules: tendency to the first stem syllable (umukwámidzi, umugosi), perfect endings on the penultimate syllable, monosyllabic stems on the last prefix syllable (umútwe).

2972.heavy: Weight does not choose the stress position; it follows from it: the foot headed by the stressed (root) syllable must be bimoraic - vowels lengthen in open syllables and before lenis codas, and fortis coda consonants (obstruents and sonorants) contribute a mora (pp. 74, 100-101); only a root with a fortis-obstruent coda before the diminutive or a clitic surfaces as a light stressed syllable in an (LL) foot (pp. 79-81, 85). Feet are moraic trochees (LL) (H).
2972.prule: One stress per (content) word, on the final syllable of the root: the head of the foot is aligned to the right edge of the root (ALIGN(Hd(Ft), R, Root, R)). Prefixes (aspect markers, animate ba-), the diminutive suffix -eʔ and pronominal enclitics are never stressed, so stress is root-final rather than word-final ([ba̰.teʔ] 'little skunk', [ɾka̰ː.zaʔ] 'I want'); in compounds the last root is stressed ([tsɨb.tjopː] 'twelve', [ɾɡwḛzakː] 'speaks well'); polysyllabic loan roots and etymologically opaque native polysyllables carry prominence on their last syllable ([ko.ɾa.sonː] 'heart'). Feet are quantity-sensitive moraic trochees, (H) or (LL): the stressed root syllable is normally bimoraic (vowel lengthening in open or lenis-coda syllables; fortis codas moraic), but a root with a fortis-obstruent coda followed by the diminutive or a clitic keeps a short vowel and heads a light-light foot ([ˈtʃa.teʔ] 'little kiss').
2972.srule: None: 'All words in this language contain only one prominent syllable (culminativity property), and thus I will assume one foot per word' (p. 81); (104a) 'Culminative: one prominent syllable per word' (p. 101). No secondary or rhythmic stress at any word length; non-root-final syllables (prefixes, diminutive -eʔ, enclitics, non-final compound roots, pretonic loanword syllables) are unstressed.

2972.tone: Quiaviní Zapotec is tonal (high, low, rising and falling tones, chs. 4-5) with contrastive phonation (modal, breathy, creaky, interrupted), and the dissertation treats stress as an independent metrical property with its own location rule; tone does not condition stress. Contour tones, phonetic long vowels, diphthongs and non-modal phonation are (near-)restricted to stressed root syllables (pp. 77-78; fn. 44 'Surface contour tones appear to be non-contrastive in unstressed syllables'). Duration is the main acoustic correlate of stress; pitch is not a cue (Chávez-Peón 2008, CLA proceedings, saved).

corr.words: The analysis is restricted to monosyllabic roots (the majority in the language). However, an important comment regarding larger domains is that tone in Quiaviní Zapotec shows little or no mobility. As long as the syllable is prominent, level and contour tones remain within the root in bigger forms. Consequently, I assume that tone is underlyingly anchored to the root.

2973.dq: The phonological word consists of a primary stress group as nucleus, optionally preceeded by up to two secondary stress groups, and optionally followed by a single post-stressed syllable.
2973.dloc: Sec. 5 'The word' (p. 20, counting the SIL cover page as p. 1; typescript pages unnumbered).
2973.prule: Primary stress falls on the nuclear (last) syllable of the word's primary stress group, which corresponds to the last free morpheme (root); up to three unstressed pre-stressed syllables precede it within the group (the non-final syllables of a polysyllabic free morpheme, e.g. na4nga4 'deep', ta3co3 'seed'; a pre-final free morpheme absorbed 'in simplified form'; and all prefixes and other bound morphemes, which never take stress and always attach as pre-stressed syllables), and at most one unstressed post-stressed syllable (a person suffix such as -no2 'you pl.') may follow it. So the primary-stressed syllable is word-final, or penultimate when a post-stressed suffix syllable closes the word; placement is stated in terms of morpheme structure (free morpheme = stress group, stressed syllable group-final), not syllable count or weight.
2973.srule: Placed by morphology: each free morpheme before the last forms a secondary stress group with secondary stress on its final (nuclear) syllable, preceded by up to three unstressed pre-stressed syllables; at most two such groups per word ('a word consisting of three free morphemes (say) will have three stressed syllables, the final stressed syllable taking primary stress and preceeding ones taking secondary stress', e.g. čhi4ne4.ški3.ni4ʔño4 'dentist', 2ary on ne4.ški3, 1ary on ni4ʔño4). A pre-final free morpheme may instead be absorbed into the primary stress group as an unstressed pre-stressed syllable (khoa4.hčą1 ~ kho4hčą1 'war'; conditions 'need more study'). Bound morphemes never take secondary stress. Secondary-stressed syllables lack the oral/nasal, interruption and ballistic/controlled contrasts (3.3.2).

2974.dq: 1.3.1. Stress. Word-level stress falls on the final syllable if closed, which is the case for most words (17a). [Contrast with phrase level, sec. 1.3.3] because underlying tonal contrasts surface only on syllables which have phrase-level stress, tone is largely a phenomenon of the phrasal phonology.
2974.dloc: Noyer preprint sec. 1.3.1 'Stress' (= ms pp. 24-25); sec. 1.3.3 'Tone', ms p. 27.
2974.heavy: Closed syllable: 'the final syllable if closed' / 'the word-final syllable if it is closed' (Noyer secs. 1.3.1, 3.1.1). Aguilar Ruiz 2019 p. 57: 'la primera sílaba pesada CVC, CVVC o CV1V2C' (all with a coda); Pak 2007 p. 312: 'final if heavy, else penultimate'. Long vowels in San Mateo Huave arise from /Vh/ only in closed syllables (Noyer sec. 1.3.2), so CVV weight is not independently testable.
2974.prule: Primary word stress falls on the final syllable if it is closed (which holds for most words), otherwise on the penult: a plainly stated closed-syllable weight rule in a two-syllable right-edge window. In native vocabulary nearly every lexical word ends in a closed syllable, so the surface pattern is almost always final stress; penult stress appears in the small set of open-final words (function words such as n′í|n′e ‘child’, i|kó|ɾa ‘we incl. dual’, kʷá|n′e ‘what?’, and recent Spanish loans).
2974.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress. Secondary stress is placed by the morphology: stress applies cyclically in derived (suffixed) words, and the syllable stressed on the last cycle (the stem-final closed syllable) keeps a secondary stress when the word-level suffixes add two or more syllables, so that it is not adjacent to the word-final primary stress (tahɨn′ ì:ʦ′asán 'we excl. cooked'); when only one syllable is added the pre-final stress is removed by Stress Clash Deletion (tahawás 'I saw'). Underived words have a single stress.

2974.tone: Noyer sec. 1.3.3 (ms p. 27): 'San Mateo is the only one of the four dialects of Huave to retain tone as a distinctive phonological property... Surface tones include high, low and falling, and because underlying tonal contrasts surface only on syllables which have phrase-level stress, tone is largely a phenomenon of the phrasal phonology. tn.quote: On the surface, the syllable with pitch accent in San Mateo Huave bears either a high (H) or falling (HL) tone. The functional load of this distinction is low, and there are only a few minimal pairs differentiated solely by tone. ... Thus, the contrast between H and HL is only found on final syllables.

2975.dq: En el quechua de San Martín una palabra fonológica se define como ± margen (región no-nuclear) realizado por uno o más acentos secundarios + núcleo realizado por un acento primario. A las palabras fonológicas también podríamos llamarlas 'grupos de acentos'. Existe una coincidencia bastante considerable entre una palabra fonológica (o 'grupos de acentos') y una palabra gramatical. (nota 2, p. 35)

2975.prule: Primary stress is obligatory and predictable: it always falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (monosyllables carry it on their only syllable). quantity-insensitive: no reference to syllable weight anywhere in the rule; sec. 2.6 (p. 30) restates 'los acentos del quechua de San Martín pueden predecirse: el acento primario aparece en la penúltima sílaba'.
2975.srule: Secondary stress (weaker) in words of four or more syllables on every second syllable counting from the first syllable of the word; in odd-length words (5+) the count starts on syllable 1 but no secondary falls on the syllable right before the penult, leaving a two-syllable lapse before the primary (e.g. ['tu.ku'tšaš.ka.ni"sa.pa] 'hemos terminado'). Two- and three-syllable words have the primary only. Variation: some speakers omit the secondary in four-syllable words; rarely the lapse follows the initial secondary instead (['ya.tša.na'ya.ni"sa.pa], p. 33).

2976.dq: Una sílaba está acentuada cuando se pronuncia con más fuerza, y tiene un tono más alto que las otras sílabas en la palabra.
2976.dloc: Lección 9 'El acento', p. 47; checked (ɨ appears as å/ã)
2976.prule: Word accent ('acento': the syllable pronounced with more force and a higher pitch than the other syllables of the word) has no stated position: in polysyllables the accented syllable must be written with an acute, and the lesson's four word pairs show a change of meaning going with a change of accent position (initial vs. penult cáanarij/canárij; initial vs. final tyéetye/tyetyéj, náavi/navíj, mɨ́'ɨchi/mɨ'ɨchí). Only mɨ́'ɨchi/mɨ'ɨchí differs by accent alone; in the other three pairs the initially-accented member also has a long vowel in the accented syllable (cáa-, tyée-, náa-) where the other member has a short vowel (and tyetyéj, navíj additionally end in -j, which both cáanarij and canárij already carry). The accent falls on the long vowel in every word that has one, a co-variation the primer does not comment on; where there is no long vowel the position varies (initial, penult, final). No default position and no weight condition is stated.

2976.tone: The primer defines the accented syllable by both greater force ('más fuerza') and higher pitch ('tono más alto') and calls it 'acento'; it says nothing about phonemic tone. For the sister Jesús María dialect (El Nayar Cora, crn/elna1235) Casad 1984:157 (read) states 'Tone is phonemic and operates partly independently of stress, which can be analyzed into primary and secondary degrees.', so a linguist's description of tereseño could recast this as pitch-accent or tone; no sant1424 source says so.

2977.dq: La acentuación de las palabras sigue las reglas del español, es decir, palabras que terminan en n, s, o una vocal, no llevan acento escrito si la penúltima sílaba es tónica.
2977.dloc: Primer: Lección 10 'El acento escrito', p.15; 'Los tonos' p.16
2977.prule: One tonic (accented) syllable per word, realised with extra vowel length; its position is not given by any rule: in some words it is the penult (nisë, nupi, guitu, shtádu', llána'), in others the final syllable (nandchí, bëcuë́, tegó, dishtí, biashtí, dumí, laní), so the orthography marks it with a written accent under Spanish conventions. No positional, weight or morphological conditioning is stated.
2977.srule: Not mentioned in Olson & Olson 1986 (Lección 10 'El acento escrito', p.15; 'Los tonos', p.16) or in Olson 1998 (sec. 0.2 'Aclaraciones', p.1; sec. 2.3.1-2.3.5, pp.10-11): both describe one tonic (accented) syllable per word and say nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
2977.quote: La acentuación de las palabras sigue las reglas del español, es decir, palabras que terminan en n, s, o una vocal, no llevan acento escrito si la penúltima sílaba es tónica. nisë agua / nupi pulque / guitu calabaza. En otras palabras la última sílaba es tónica y lleva acento escrito. nandchí hoy / bëcuë́ soplador. Palabras que terminan en saltillo o consonante que no sea n, o s, llevan acento si la penúltima sílaba es tónica. shtádu' tu padre / llána' mi madre. [Grammar sec. 0.2, p.1] Las vocales sencillas que llevan el acento tienen un sonido más largo que las otras: dumí dinero / laní fiest…

2977.idn: zapoteco de Santa Inez Yatzeche, Oax. (primer); 'Santa Inés Yatzechi (Southeastern Zimatlán)' per the grammar's archive title, grammar typescript headed 'ZPN-28599'; data: Santa Inez Yatzeche, Oaxaca; primer prepared by Donald and Anne Olson 'con la colaboración de hablantes del zapoteco de Santa Inez', published…
2977.tone: Both sources describe lexical tone on every syllable alongside the accent. Grammar sec. 0.2: 'En zapoteco cada sílaba tiene su propio tono, pero éste no se indica en forma escrita.' Primer p.16 'Los tonos': minimal pairs guidë (bajo-bajo) cuero vs guidë (ascendiente-bajo) gallina; be'u (alto-alto) luna vs be'u (alto-bajo) pulga; lli'ilë (alto-alto) borrego vs lli'ilë (bajo-alto) algodón; 'en la ortografía normal los tonos no se escriben'. The accent ('acento', tonic syllable, longer vowel) is described as a separate property from tone, so this is a stress statement in a tonal language, not a tone-only system.

tn.quote: Los tonos. Hay algunas palabras que se escriben con las mismas letras pero se distinguen porque sus tonos son diferentes, como en los siguientes ejemplos. Los tonos están indicados entre paréntesis. guidë (bajo - bajo) cuero / guidë (ascendiente - bajo) gallina / bë'u (alto - alto) luna / bë'u (alto - bajo) pulga / lli'ilë (alto - alto) borrego / lli'ilë (bajo - alto) algodón. En zapoteco la mayoría de las palabras se distinguen por las letras con que se escriben sin tomar en cuenta el tono. Por eso, en la ortografía normal los tonos no se escriben.
tn.translation: Tones. There are some words that are written with the same letters but are distinguished because their tones are different, as in the following examples. The tones are indicated in parentheses. guidë (low - low) 'leather' / guidë (rising - low) 'hen' / bë'u (high - high) 'moon' / bë'u (high - low) 'flea' / lli'ilë (high - high) 'sheep' / lli'ilë (low - high) 'cotton'. In Zapotec most words are distinguished by the letters they are written with, without taking tone into account. Therefore, in the normal orthography the tones are not written.

2981.dq: Every phonological word is parsed into moraic trochees, and the leftmost foot is accorded primary stress. The stress of each subsequent foot is then subordinated into alternating secondary stresses. [§7.1, p. 83] ... The leftmost stress in a noun phrase is accorded the highest amount of prominence, and each successive stress—even across three or more words—is subordinated to this primary stress. …
2981.dloc: Thesis ch. 6 Prosody, §6.1 Word-level stress, pp. 70-75: deciding sentences p. 70, p. 72, p. 73, vowel-weight hierarchy p. 74, exceptions pp. 73 and 75 (98); §6.3 Phrasal stress p. 78; §7.1 p. 83. E-book: §6.1 p. 76, hierarchy (24) p. 82.
2981.heavy: Heavy = a syllable with a coda consonant (quantity-sensitivity) and/or a more open, more sonorous vowel nucleus (quality-sensitivity) on the hierarchy /a/ > /e o/ > /ə/ > /i u/ > /ɨ/; weight is relative ('heavier'), and 'The most important property for determining the weight of syllables in Ma Manda is vowel aperture' (p. 73). Foot = (ĹL) or (H́). No vowel-length contrast is invoked.
2981.dflt: Word-initial (leftmost syllable): 'In the default case, Ma Manda has word-initial stress'; two light syllables with the same nucleus quality are ĹL, e.g. [qə́.wə] 'in-law', [mú.su] 'yam sp.', [qé.qe] 'roots' (p. 70).
2981.prule: Left-headed moraic trochees (ĹL) or (H́) parsed left-to-right; the leftmost foot carries primary stress, so the default is word-initial stress. A heavier second (sometimes third) syllable — heavier by a coda consonant (quantity) or by a more open/sonorous vowel on the scale /a/ > /e o/ > /ə/ > /i u/ > /ɨ/ (quality) — pulls primary stress away from a lighter initial syllable; the author calls the system unbounded. Stress is non-contrastive but 'not entirely predictable'.
2981.srule: Secondary stress on the head of each non-primary moraic trochee (feet parsed left-to-right), subordinated to the leftmost primary stress and typically on alternating syllables, complicated by heavy syllables and stress clash: [qó.bɨ.sè] 'chicken', [sén.da.pòq] 'cocoon', [qé.lɨ.nə̀] 'hand-1SG.POSS'; when a heavier syllable to the right takes the primary, the initial foot keeps secondary stress, (L̀L)(H́) [qù.su.wə́t] 'tree sp.', [lə̀.gə.mán.dɨ] 'dream'. Author's hedge: 'it is debatable whether there is any reliable distinction between primary and secondary stresses'; acoustic confirmation left to future research (iterativity 'cannot as yet be proven', Pennington 2014: 89).

Ist dieselbe lang, so hat sie den Ictus-Accent'. Pischel does not define heaviness; in Latin and Sanskrit prosody a syllable is long by nature (long vowel) or by position (closed).

2984.prule: Pischel 1900 § 46: in Śaurasenī (with Māgadhī and Ḍhakkī) the accent of classical Sanskrit, 'which mostly agrees with that of Latin', is demonstrable, beside residues of the Vedic (lexical) accent; Pischel KZ 34: 574-575 grounds this in the long-vowel and geminate forms of the prose dialects, which point to the later accent. The Latin-type rule this implies, Pischel's own claim: ictus on the penult if long, otherwise on the antepenult. Pischel's opponent Jacobi (1893: 574-575, cited by Pischel under 'Anders'), reporting via Bühler the modern pronunciation of Sanskrit and projecting it onto Pali and Prakrit, adds retraction to the fourth-last when the antepenult is also short and stem-stress in verbs; Jacobi KZ 35: 563 calls the Middle Indic accent an expiratory one 'dependent on the quantity of the penult or antepenult'. For the prose dialect Śaurasenī both camps therefore give a right-edge quantity accent; they differ on whether Vedic-accent residues exist beside it. The accent is predominantly expiratory (stress), not purely musical. The whole statement is a philological inference from vowel length, syncope and gemination in a dead literary language; no accent is written or described by native grammarians.

2985.dq: The general rule for stress in roots in a one- or two-word sentence where the bare root is used is that the penultimate syllable of a root carries primary stress (marked by ˈ in the examples).
2985.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.3 Stress and 2.3.1 Root stress, pp. 24-25; Table 2.6 p. 25; sec. 2.3.2 Influence of affixes and clitics on stress, pp. 26-28, Table 2.7 p. 28.
2985.heavy: Not applicable: 'Both V and CV syllables can take primary or secondary stress' and 'syllable structure does not have an influence on stress assignment' (p. 25). No closed syllables or vowel-length contrast figure in the rule.
2985.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root, counted from the right edge ('stress assignment proceeds from the end of the root'), quantity-insensitive. Holds without exception for disyllabic roots (initial = penult) and for four-syllable roots; for trisyllabic roots it is the majority pattern (about 75% of 292) with an unpredictable 25% stressed on the initial syllable. Roots of five or more syllables are historically complex and combine the patterns of their parts (no single position stated).
2985.srule: Secondary stress on the root-initial syllable whenever primary stress is non-initial, '(almost) as prominent as the primarily stressed syllable': penult-stressed trisyllabic roots ˌσˈσσ (ˌaˈgutu 'work'), four-syllable roots ˌσσˈσσ (ˌkenaˈghuli 'fishing hook'); no secondary stress in disyllabic or initial-stressed trisyllabic roots. The rightmost stressed syllable is analysed as primary; secondary shows 'usually no or only little difference in realization'. Reduplicated forms likewise take secondary stress on the first syllable (sec. 2.4.2).

2987.tone: Voorhoeve 1971 raises only 'the possibility of phonemic pitch': most long-vowel words carry a falling-rising contour on the final syllable, but five words (ko:d, mu:d, a:r, sir, a:p) show a level contour consistently across the three recordings. tn.quote: Pitch contours: typical for most of the words with a long vowel is a falling-rising pitch contour on the last syllable. 2988.prule: Primary stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable of the word (heavy = a syllable whose nucleus is V:, Vʔ or Vh) (Wichmann's rule Sa/1a); if the word has no heavy syllable, on the leftmost syllable of the rightmost root (Sa/1b); certain inherently accented suffixes, inflectional (-wáy 'diminutive', -kits 'pl. descending', áh ~ -ám 'future') and derivational (-húgum 'inside', -húk 'extensive', -it 'condition'), override the pattern (Sa/2); Spanish loans keep the stress of the donor language and are not affected by Sa/1 (Sa/3) (Wichmann 1995: 81, an analysis of Clark's 1961 data, stated as rules 'still easily discernible from the data' in a language that 'verge[s] toward having phonemic stress', the phonemicity being 'due to the lexicalization of formerly derivational processes and to the historical merging of compounds into unanalyzable simplex forms'; restated by van der Hulst, Rice & Wetzels 2010: 273).
2988.srule: Tentative rule (Wichmann): 'Secondary stress seems to be assigned cyclically according to the same rules as primary stress [rightmost heavy syllable, else leftmost syllable of the rightmost root], provided that there are at least two syllables between the syllable carrying primary stress and the one receiving secondary stress. Such a possibility arises only in tri- and tetra-syllabic stems. Since examples are scanty, this rule must be tentative.'

2989.dq: 韻律特徴は、その性格上、複音節語（音韻語）の初頭２音節（声調が機能する単位）に対してのみ適用される。[p.2] ... 複音節語について語単独での発音では、第１音節に聴覚印象として明瞭な強勢が置かれる例が存在する。[p.9, quoting Suzuki 2012d:60]
2989.dloc: Suzuki 2013: p.2 (end of §1 and the §2 bullet summary), p.4 (§3.1 first lines), p.9 (§4.1, quoting Suzuki 2012d:60 on mBalhag), p.10 (§4.1 end), p.11 (§5 summary table). Supporting: Suzuki 2012 (国立民族学博物館研究報告 37(1)) §2.2 p.60; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 §7.3.3-7.3.4 pp.241-243.
2989.prule: Word-tone language: four pitch patterns (high level, rising, falling, rising-falling) realised over the first two syllables of the phonological word; syllables 3+ are 'light' (軽声, toneless, low level). No phonetically prominent, phonologically functional word stress in the group as a whole (sDerong, West Yunling Mountain and sPomtserag subgroups): stress never appears with phonetic prominence and cannot be said to function in the sound system; an abstract, explicitly non-phonological iambic (weak-strong) 'prosodic feature' over syllables 1-2 is inferred only from segmental weakening of syllable 1 (deaspiration, /a/ reduction) at natural speech rate. mBalhag subgroup only (trochaic type): an optional, non-contrastive, free-variation audible stress on syllable 1 of polysyllabic words in isolation, never on syllable 2 or later (Suzuki 2012d:60). gYagrwa subgroup: neither prosodic type needed (指定不要).
2989.srule: None: at most one stress per word. mBalhag subgroup: optional, non-contrastive stress on syllable 1 only, 「第２音節以降に強勢が置かれる例は認められない」 (no stress ever on syllable 2 or later); rest of the group: 「強勢が音声学的な卓立を伴って現れることはない」 (stress never surfaces with phonetic prominence) and none on syllable 2; syllables 3+ light/toneless. Secondary stress is not discussed as such.
2989.quote: 本稿で議論するカムチベット語諸方言では、強勢が音声学的な卓立を伴って現れることはないため、強勢が音体系上機能していると言うことができない。超分節音的音特徴にはおよそ明瞭な強勢の特徴が認められず、逆にチベット言語学上奇妙な現象が分節音に起きている。この現象を説明するために、「強さを伴わない架空の強勢パターン」（これを韻律特徴と呼ぶ）を設けて議論してみる。[...] • カムチベット語得榮徳欽方言群の諸方言は、基本的に「弱強型」の韻律特徴をもつ。•「弱強型」の韻律特徴は、第１音節の分節音に何らかの変化が生じる。• ただし、例外的に「強弱型」の韻律特徴をもつ方言を認める。•「強弱型」の韻律特徴は、第１音節に強勢が実際に置かれることで実現することが多い。韻律特徴は、その性格上、複音節語（音韻語）の初頭２音節（声調が機能する単位）に対してのみ適用される。[p.4] いずれの２音節語の場合も第２音節に強勢が音声学的に強さを伴って現れることはない。また、３音節以上からなる場合にもこの現象が現れることがあるが、３音節以降は軽声であるため無視できる。[p.9, quoting 鈴木 2012d:60 on mBalhag:] 複音節語について語単独での発音では、第１音節に聴覚印象として明瞭な強勢が置かれる例が存在する。強勢が置かれた場合、その直後すなわち第２音節以降の声調が低平調で実現される。また…

2989.exq_: しかしながら、強勢の実現は現段階の資料において対立が認められず、かつ自由変異であり、現れても現れなくても許容されるため、一律表記しない。[p.9] ... いずれにせよ語幹でないものが第１音節に来ている形式には「強弱型」はあまり現れないのであるが、語構成が「語幹＋接尾辞」のものすべてが「強弱型」を取るとは限らないため、規則性があるとはいえない。[p.10]
2989.tone: Distinctive suprasegmental is word tone: four patterns (高平調 high level, 上昇調 rising, 下降調 falling, 上昇下降調 rising-falling) formed on syllables 1-2 of the word, syllable 3+ realised at about [22] (Suzuki 2012 Minpaku 37(1): 60 §2.2; same statement in Tsharethong AALL 7 §3, Sakar RIHN 4 §3, sPomtserag AALL 4, Bodgrong AALL 9, rTserong KULR 44 §2.4, gYagrwa KULR 41). On stress, Suzuki 2013 p.2: stress never appears accompanied by phonetic prominence, so it cannot be said to function in the sound system; fn.2: in almost all pitch-tone Tibetic varieties stress is expected to have no suprasegmental phonetic realisation, and the term 'stress' is used only where a clear suprasegmental feature is attested. Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 §7.3.3 p.242: Yunnan Kham dialects Tormarong and mBalhag 'show a prominent stress as a phonetic status', ex. mBalhag SOL.BA 'coal' /ɬeːja/ (no stress) vs SRING.MO 'younger sister' /`ɬiwũ/, but 'the stress is a secondary feature... and the pitch pattern is fundamental'; §7.3.4 p.243: 'Some dialects of Southern Kham have an iambic prosodic pattern (weak-strong) for the first two syllables (Suzuki 2013b)'.

tn.quote: mBalhag 方言の超分節音は，ピッチの高低による対立で実現され，高平調，上昇調，下降調，上昇下降調の 4 種に分かれる。弁別的なのは現れるピッチの高さ（調値）ではなく，平板か上昇もしくは下降などの型（調類）である。声調は語単位でかかるが，3 音節以上の語の場合，第 1，第 2 音節までで弁別的な声調の型を形成し，第 3 音節以降は [22] 程度の高さで現れる。つまり，複音節語では各音節が独自の声調を持たず，語ごとにパターンが決まっている。
tn.translation: The suprasegmentals of the mBalhag dialect are realised as an opposition of pitch height and divide into 4 types: high level, rising, falling and rising-falling. What is distinctive is not the pitch height that appears (tone value) but the pattern (tone category), i.e. level vs rising or falling etc. Tone applies to the word as a unit, but in words of 3 or more syllables the distinctive tone pattern is formed over syllables 1-2, and syllable 3 onward appears at a height of about [22]. That is, in polysyllabic words each syllable does not carry its own tone; the pattern is fixed word by word.
tn.cite: Suzuki Hiroyuki 2012, カムチベット語香格里拉県巴拉[mBalhag]方言の方言特徴, 国立民族学博物館研究報告 37(1): 53-90, §2.1-2.2 (quoted); also read: Suzuki 2013 RIHN5 (primary) §1-2, fn.2, §4.1, fn.20; Suzuki 2012 Sakar RIHN4 §3.1-3.2; Suzuki 2025 rTserong KULR44 §2.4

tn.note: Word-tone system: each phonological word takes one of four melodies (high level, rising, falling, rising-falling) over syllables 1-2; later syllables low [22]. Same system given for Sakar, rTserong. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): evidence elicitation -> impressionistic (§1.3 p.57; §1.2 p.56; §2.2 p.60).

2990.prule: Stress consistently on the final syllable of the word ('consistently word-final'; 'word-final stress'), stated as an areal feature of the Malayic Dayak / Ibanic languages of the Kapuas River area and applied explicitly to Seberuang as the cause of its allophonic final high-vowel breaking (kutu [kutow], tali [taley]). No weight condition, no schwa condition, no secondary stress mentioned.
2990.srule: Not mentioned in Smith 2017, sec. 2.8.2-2.8.2.2 (pp. 185-187): the source gives only word-final (primary) stress for Seberuang and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
2990.quote: The Ibanic languages, Seberuang, Mualang, and Iban (specifically the Iban of the Kapuas River, not the Iban of Sarawak), and other Malayic Dayak languages have undergone several areal adaptations which have altered their phonologies.
